results.name: four_minus_two_example_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on 4-example sets minus yes-rate on 2-example sets; observed > model means people narrow their generalisation with more examples less than the size principle predicts (observed < model: they narrow more).

results.name: shared_last_digit_contrast
results.description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share one last digit, yes-rate for targets with that last digit minus yes-rate for targets without it; observed < model means people's last-digit generalisation is less sharp (they accept non-matching or reject matching targets more) than the model's "ends in d" rule predicts.
results.code:
# name: shared_last_digit_contrast
# description: Among sets of >=2 examples that all share one last digit, yes-rate for targets with that last digit minus yes-rate for targets without it; observed < model means people's last-digit generalisation is less sharp (they accept non-matching or reject matching targets more) than the model's "ends in d" rule predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(sets), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(sets, 10)
    first = ld[:, 0]
    same = np.all((ld == first[:, None]) | np.isnan(ld), axis=1) & (n >= 2)
    tld = np.mod(df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy(), 10)
    match = tld == first
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a, b = same & match, same & ~match
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: participant_yes_rate_sd
results.description: SD across participants (blocks inferred from trial_index resets; all see the same 450 items) of the overall yes-rate; observed > model means people differ in baseline yes-bias/generalisation breadth that the single shared-parameter model does not produce.

results.name: odd_set_parity_contrast
results.description: Among sets whose examples are all odd but do not share a last digit, yes-rate for odd targets minus yes-rate for even targets; observed < model means people generalise the "odd" concept less (or rely on other features) than the model's parity rule predicts; observed > model means stronger parity generalisation.
results.code:
# name: odd_set_parity_contrast
# description: Among sets whose examples are all odd but do not share a last digit, yes-rate for odd targets minus yes-rate for even targets; observed < model means people generalise the "odd" concept less (or rely on other features) than the model's parity rule predicts; observed > model means stronger parity generalisation.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(sets), axis=1)
    allodd = np.all((np.mod(sets, 2) == 1) | np.isnan(sets), axis=1)
    ld = np.mod(sets, 10)
    same_ld = np.all((ld == ld[:, [0]]) | np.isnan(ld), axis=1)
    sel = allodd & ~same_ld & (n >= 2)
    todd = np.mod(df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy(), 2) == 1
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    a, b = sel & todd, sel & ~todd
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: outside_range_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate among targets lying outside [min, max] of the example set; observed > model means people extend generalisation beyond the examples' range more than the model's intervals/rules allow (observed < model: people are more range-bound).

results.name: proximity_gradient
results.description: Yes-rate for targets within 5 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets more than 20 from the nearest example; observed > model means people generalise by numeric similarity/magnitude more steeply than the rule+interval posterior predicts.
results.code:
# name: proximity_gradient
# description: Yes-rate for targets within 5 of the nearest example minus yes-rate for targets more than 20 from the nearest example; observed > model means people generalise by numeric similarity/magnitude more steeply than the rule+interval posterior predicts.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).astype(float).to_numpy()
    tgt = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    dist = np.nanmin(np.abs(sets - tgt[:, None]), axis=1)
    r = df["rating"].to_numpy().astype(float)
    near, far = dist <= 5, dist > 20
    if near.sum() == 0 or far.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[near].mean() - r[far].mean())

results.name: late_minus_early_yes_rate
results.description: Yes-rate on trials with trial_index >= 225 minus yes-rate on earlier trials; a nonzero observed value vs model (which has no time dependence) means people become more (positive) or less (negative) liberal over the session.

results.name: response_repetition_lag1
results.description: Within-participant (blocks from trial_index resets) P(yes | previous trial yes) minus P(yes | previous trial no); observed > model means sequential response perseveration/inertia beyond what stimulus-driven model probabilities produce.
